theodore-roosevelt.summary: Three separate units of grassy badlands along the Little Missouri River, where striped buttes rise above cottonwood bottoms and bison graze in the open. Theodore Roosevelt came here to ranch in the 1880s, and the landscape that shaped his conservation views is still wide, quiet, and easy to move through at your own pace.
theodore-roosevelt.whyGo: You can see bison, prairie dogs, and wild horses in a single morning, then walk a ridge above the river without meeting anyone.
highlights: Bison and wild horses on the prairie
River Bend Overlook in the North Unit

dayPlan.morning: Start in the South Unit, driving the scenic loop slowly while the light is low and animals are feeding. Stop at pullouts rather than rushing the whole circuit.
dayPlan.afternoon: Walk a short trail out from a viewpoint, then drive north to the North Unit if you have the time. Its overlooks look over a greener, steeper stretch of badlands.
dayPlan.evening: Find a rise with a western view and let the buttes go blue as the sun drops. Stay out for stars; this is ranch country with very little light around it.

theodore-roosevelt.seasonNote: Summer is hot and exposed, with little shade on the trails. Late spring and early autumn bring cooler walking, and winter leaves the units nearly empty but snow can close roads.
theodore-roosevelt.tip: Drive with patience near bison, give them room, and keep a full water bottle with you; the badlands dry out fast in the afternoon.

virgin-islands.summary: Most of this park covers the north shore of St. John, where steep green hills drop into clear water and beaches sit at the bottom of short trails. You come here to swim, snorkel over coral, and walk to plantation ruins in the shade of the forest.
virgin-islands.whyGo: Warm water, reef fish within a few strokes of shore, and trails that end at sand instead of a parking lot.
highlights: Lind Point Trail above the water

dayPlan.morning: Get to a north shore beach early, before the day heats up, and swim out over the reef with a mask. Shade is scarce on the sand, so claim a spot under the trees.
dayPlan.afternoon: Walk the Lind Point trail for views back over the harbor, or follow a path inland to old estate ruins. Move slowly; the hills are short but steep.
dayPlan.evening: Return to the water for a late swim, then find a west-facing overlook as the sun goes down. Dinner in town finishes the day.

virgin-islands.seasonNote: The park is warm year-round, but late summer and autumn are the wettest stretch. Winter and spring bring drier, breezier days and calmer water for snorkeling.
virgin-islands.tip: Bring reef-safe sunscreen and your own snorkel gear if you can; shade, water, and equipment are limited once you leave the trailhead.

voyageurs.summary: A water park of connected lakes and wooded islands along the northern Minnesota border, with granite shorelines and a sky that opens up at night. Nearly everything here happens from a boat, so you plan around water rather than trails.
voyageurs.whyGo: You can paddle between wooded islands all day, then watch the northern lights come up over the same shoreline after dark.

dayPlan.morning: Launch early while the lakes are still glassy, following a shoreline toward one of the rock gardens or a quiet bay. Watch for loons and beavers near the reeds.
dayPlan.afternoon: Anchor for a swim and a slow lunch on an island, then fish a drop-off or explore a second bay. Afternoon wind usually builds, so keep the return trip short.
dayPlan.evening: Find a west-facing rock point for sunset, then stay put as the stars come out. On clear nights the aurora can appear low on the northern horizon.

voyageurs.seasonNote: Open water draws most visitors, but winter turns parts of the lakes into marked ice routes for skiing and snowshoeing. Spring and autumn are quiet, cold, and changeable.
voyageurs.tip: Check the wind forecast before you commit to a long crossing, and carry a map; islands look alike once you are out among them.

white-sands.summary: A field of white gypsum dunes fills part of the Tularosa Basin, soft enough to walk barefoot and bright enough to change color as the light moves. There is no rim to reach or long trail to follow here; you drive in, park, and wander.
white-sands.whyGo: You come for the sensation of walking on soft white sand under a wide desert sky, with mountains standing along the horizon.

dayPlan.morning: Arrive early when the sand is cool and shadows are long, and walk out away from the road until the footprints thin. Bring water; the glare is strong.
dayPlan.afternoon: Find a steep face and try sledding, or follow a marked trail between the dunes. Rest through the brightest hours if the heat builds.
dayPlan.evening: Stay for sunset, when low light turns the sand pink and the mountains go dark. The drive out is easy and the sky stays bright for a while.

white-sands.seasonNote: Summer afternoons are fierce, so plan around morning and evening. Spring and autumn bring milder temperatures, and winter dunes are cold but often clear and nearly empty.
white-sands.tip: Wear sunglasses and a hat, carry more water than you think you need, and note a landmark before you wander; dunes hide the road quickly.

wind-cave.summary: Below a rolling prairie in the southern Black Hills, Wind Cave holds a network of passages lined with boxwork, the thin calcite fins that give ceilings a honeycomb pattern. Above ground, bison and prairie dogs share open grass with hikers working the ridges.
wind-cave.whyGo: You can spend the morning underground in a cool cave and the afternoon on a warm ridge watching bison move through the grass.
highlights: Boxwork ceilings on a cave tour
Prairie dog towns beside the road

dayPlan.morning: Join a cave tour in the morning and dress for steady cool temperatures underground. Look up often, since most of the boxwork is overhead.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive the prairie roads looking for bison and prairie dog towns, then walk up Rankin Ridge for a wide view over the hills and grass.
dayPlan.evening: Stay out as the light softens and animals move again after the heat. The prairie horizon is low and open, so sunset lasts.

wind-cave.seasonNote: The cave stays cool whatever the season, so bring a layer even in summer. Prairie trails are hot and exposed in July, while spring brings green grass and calmer weather.
wind-cave.tip: Book a cave tour before you arrive if you can, and carry a jacket; the underground air stays cold enough to notice in shorts.

wrangell-st-elias.summary: A vast Alaskan park and preserve of glacier-covered mountains, wide river valleys, and one historic copper mining town at the end of a long road. Most of it is roadless, so even a short visit feels like standing at the edge of something much larger.
wrangell-st-elias.whyGo: You can walk to the face of a glacier in the morning and stand among abandoned mill buildings in the afternoon.

dayPlan.morning: Drive in to Kennecott and walk the old mill town while the valley is still in shadow. The buildings sit against a wall of mountain and glacier.
dayPlan.afternoon: Take a guided walk toward the Root Glacier, or hike a valley trail if you are comfortable navigating without signs. Conditions change fast.
dayPlan.evening: Eat simply and sleep early; the light lasts late in summer and mornings are the calmest part of the day. Look up for stars if the sky clears.

wrangell-st-elias.seasonNote: Visitor services run mainly in summer, when roads are open and days are long. Spring and autumn are short and wet, and winter access is limited to those prepared for deep snow.
wrangell-st-elias.tip: Carry food, water, and rain gear for the whole day, and treat every distance as longer than it looks on the map.

yellowstone.summary: The first national park, spread across three states on a high volcanic plateau where geysers, hot springs, and mud pots steam among lodgepole forest and open valleys. Bison, elk, and wolves live here in numbers large enough that wildlife often sets the pace of your day.
yellowstone.whyGo: Geothermal basins, a huge lake, and open valleys full of bison sit close enough together that one day can hold all three.
highlights: Geysers in the Upper Geyser Basin
Steam and color at Mammoth Hot Springs

dayPlan.morning: Start early in the geyser basins while steam is thick and boardwalks are quiet, then drive through Lamar Valley to look for bison and wolves.
dayPlan.afternoon: Walk a canyon rim or a lakeshore trail away from the main pullouts, keeping your distance from any animal that is close to the path.
dayPlan.evening: Sit by a hot spring as the light fades and the air cools, then stay for stars. Night brings animals onto the roads, so drive slowly.

yellowstone.seasonNote: Summer is busy and warm, with afternoon storms. Late spring and early autumn bring cooler air and active animals, and winter quiets the roads but limits access.
yellowstone.tip: Keep well back from bison and elk, stay on boardwalks in thermal areas, and give yourself more time than the map suggests for animal traffic.

yosemite.summary: Granite walls rise straight out of Yosemite Valley, with waterfalls dropping into the Merced River and high meadows opening farther east. The park is large enough that the valley, the giant sequoias, and the quiet high country feel like separate trips.
yosemite.whyGo: You can stand under a waterfall in the morning and be alone in a high meadow by afternoon, all inside one park.
highlights: Yosemite Falls from the valley floor

dayPlan.morning: Walk the valley floor early, when the light reaches the north wall and the paths are still cool. Choose one waterfall and take it slowly.
dayPlan.afternoon: Drive up to Glacier Point for the wide view, or head east toward Tuolumne Meadows for open subalpine country and cooler air.
dayPlan.evening: Return to the valley for the last light on Half Dome, or stay high and watch the ridge line fade. Walk to a meadow edge for stars.

yosemite.seasonNote: Late spring brings heavy waterfall runoff and lingering snow up high. Summer is warm and crowded in the valley, and autumn clears out while the high country turns gold.
yosemite.tip: Park once and walk or use the valley shuttle rather than moving the car, and carry water; the granite holds the afternoon heat.

zion.summary: A deep sandstone canyon in southern Utah, where the Virgin River runs along the floor and tall red walls close in on both sides. Trails range from flat riverside walks to steep climbs, and the light on the rock changes all day.
zion.whyGo: You can walk in the river between canyon walls in the morning and watch the same walls glow at sunset.
highlights: The Narrows up the Virgin River
Towers of the Virgin at sunset

dayPlan.morning: Ride the canyon shuttle early and walk the riverside path toward the Narrows while the canyon is still cool and shaded.
dayPlan.afternoon: Climb a switchback trail for a view over the valley, or drive up to Kolob Canyons for a quieter side of the park. Take the heat seriously.
dayPlan.evening: Find a west-facing bench and watch the towers turn orange, then walk back along the river as the canyon empties out.

zion.seasonNote: Spring and autumn bring mild days and the clearest walking weather. Summer afternoons are hot, and winter can leave ice on shaded trails high above the river.
zion.tip: Start early to stay ahead of the heat and the crowds, and check the water level before you commit to walking in the river.
